components.gap: Durrett presents this computation as Example 4.1.8, Borel's paradox (p. 210): at first glance both the longitude theta and the great-circle angle phi should be uniform; theta is uniform but phi is not; the paradox evaporates because phi is independent of theta in either parametrization, so the conditional law is the unconditional one, nonuniform because there is more land near the equator than near the North Pole. The handbook (body 222-248, annex 346-389) proves the independence and the |cos psi|/4 density, but never names Borel's paradox, states the naive uniform expectation, or gives the source's equator explanation; the only route mention of the Borel paradox (bayes-factor-computation line 1041) is unrelated and unlinked.

resolution: the angle is independent of the longitude in either parametrization, so the conditional law equals the unconditional one, nonuniform because more of the sphere lies near the equator than near the pole

components.gap: The source's existence caveat (p. 214) is not fully preserved: regular conditional distributions do not always exist, the first example being due to Dieudonne (1948) (see Doob 1953, p. 624, or Faden 1985), and the stated reason that although P(X in union A_n | G) = sum_n P(X in A_n | G) a.s. for disjoint A_n, the exceptional sets may pile up when S contains enough countable disjoint families. The boundary (body 250-257) only says existence is not asserted beyond standard Borel targets, and def:p15-w02b-p15-008-limits item 3 records the bare non-existence statement; the Dieudonne attribution, the references and the pile-up explanation appear nowhere on the route.

components.gap: The source's claims framing this generalization (p. 53) are omitted: Theorem 2.1.21 is not valid for arbitrary measurable spaces, the first counterexample (an infinite product of different spaces) being due to Andersen and Jessen (1948) (see Halmos 1950, p. 214; Neveu 1965, p. 84), with an example using identical factor spaces in Wegner (1973).
